newsitem.title: THAILAND: Rate cuts won't hurt Thai bank earnings - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Rate cuts won't hurt Thai bank earnings - analysts.

text.p: The small cuts in deposit and lending rates made by major Thai banks this week are unlikely to have a big impact on the banking sector's earnings, analysts said on Wednesday.
More damaging to earnings could be the billions of dollars in non-performing loans Thai financial institutions had made to the depressed and cash-strapped property sector, they told Reuters.

Several major banks, including Thailand's largest commercial bank Bangkok Bank, this week cut their lending and deposit rates by at least 25 basis points. The cuts followed a Bank of Thailand signal that it may be appropriate to ease current high rates.

But the rate cuts failed to impress the stock market where investors considered the reductions too small to spur the slow economy and expressed concerns that bank earnings could suffer due to anticipated lower interest income.
The bourse tumbled by more than two percent on Tuesday to a new 1997 low as investors dumped bank shares on those concerns.
Thai rates are still among the highest in the region, ranging from 12.75-13.00 percent, despite this week's cuts.
"The interest rate cut will certainly have some impact on their (banks') earnings, but very minimal," said Philip Gawsawadikul, banking analyst at ABN-Amro Huare Govett Asia.
"The profit margins of most banks have already been narrowing sharply, not because of the interest rate reduction, but mainly due to the increase in their non-performing loans," he said.
Commercial banks' non-performing loans have risen sharply as the slowing economy had affected corporate earnings and the ability of businesses to repay loans, analysts said.
They also said further cuts in local rates might not significantly boost overall bank lending because the sagging economy had reduced demand for funds to make new investments.

"The rate cut will just provide support, I don't think it will help much. There might not be many borrowers around there because the economic outlook is very fragile," said Jimmy Koh, an economist at think-tank I.D.E.A. in Singapore.
Thailand officially expects the national economy to grow by 6.8 percent this year, after growth slumped below double digits after nearly a decade to 6.7 percent in 1996.

But some private analysts see growth braking to below six percent this year as weak exports, slowing private and manufacturing activity as well as turmoil in the financial and property sectors take their toll on the economy.
Analysts expected most banks to announce sharply lower profits this year on higher provisioning they would have to make for expected increases in non-performing loans.
The central bank last month ordered banks to raise provisioning for sub-standard assets, in addition to routine provisions, as it moved to revamp the troubled finance sector.
The prolonged slump in the property sector, which has shown no signs of recovery yet, could force developers to default on repayments and dent bank earnings, analysts said.
"Banks' earnings are already going to be hurt. It's almost certain that bank earnings in 1997 are going to be very low," said one analyst at a foreign brokerage house.

Koh at I.D.E.A. expected another 25 basis points cut in Thai interest rates in the next few weeks, but any sharper reductions could be stemmed by the central bank's policy of keeping rates high to defend the baht from speculative attacks.
